For someone interested in computer architecture, this entire story can be viewed from another angle.
A processor is a system of interacting layers. The same is true of the semiconductor industry.

Architecture depends on implementation. Implementation depends on manufacturing. Manufacturing depends on equipment and materials. Equipment depends on specialized engineering. All of these depend on people, capital, software and research.
Remove one layer and the behavior of the whole system can change.

This is exactly the kind of problem that systems thinking is designed to understand. The interesting question is not simply 'Who makes the best chip?' It is 'What network of dependencies makes the chip possible?'
The future may belong to the connectors
The semiconductor industry is often portrayed through famous companies and famous processors. But some of the most consequential technologies sit between the obvious layers.

Packaging connects dies. Interconnects connect processors and memory. EDA tools connect designs to manufacturing. Instruction sets connect software to hardware. Standards connect companies. Universities connect theory to engineering. Supply chains connect countries.
These interfaces are where dependencies become visible.
And interfaces are where new opportunities often appear.
A different definition of semiconductor power
Semiconductor power is therefore not a single number. It is not merely the number of fabs a country owns, the number of chips it exports, or the size of its semiconductor companies.
It is the ability to understand, design, manufacture, verify, package, deploy and improve computing technology across multiple layers of the stack.

That is why the semiconductor contest reaches from atomic-scale manufacturing to instruction-set architecture, from chemical engineering to operating systems, and from university laboratories to national industrial policy.
The chip is tiny.
The system surrounding it is enormous.
And the competition is increasingly about who can understand that entire system well enough to shape what comes next.

The future of computing will not be decided only by who designs the fastest processor. It will also be shaped by who can build the factories, control the tools, train the engineers, develop the architectures, secure the supply chains and preserve the knowledge required to keep those processors possible.
The war for semiconductors is therefore not really a war over silicon.
It is a competition over the ability to turn knowledge into computing power.

title: Algorithmic Humans
excerpt: Algorithms increasingly decide who gets noticed, approved, shortlisted, admitted, or investigated. They do not need to make the final decision to shape it. The difficult questions are no longer only technical: what data should a system use, what does fairness mean, who is accountable when it fails, and when should humans refuse to let an algorithm decide?

body.text: A person applies for a job. Another applies for a loan. Someone else applies to university. In each case, the decision may appear to belong to a human institution: a company, a bank, or an admissions office. Increasingly, however, software participates somewhere in the process.

The system may rank applications, estimate risk, detect patterns, recommend candidates, filter information, or decide which cases deserve human attention. The machine does not always make the final decision. It does not have to. Once its output determines what a human sees, the algorithm has already entered the decision.
This is the central problem of algorithmic decision-making: people are increasingly being evaluated through systems that transform human lives into data, predictions, scores, and rankings.
From people to predictions
An algorithm does not see a person in the way another person does. It sees a representation.

A job applicant becomes education, experience, skills, previous employment, test results, location, and other measurable attributes. A borrower becomes financial history, income, repayment records, debt, and other variables. A student becomes grades, test scores, application information, and characteristics derived from their educational history.
Machine learning systems operate on these representations. They identify statistical relationships and use them to produce predictions.
That distinction matters because prediction is not understanding. A system can predict that someone resembles people who previously succeeded without knowing why those people succeeded.
The model can discover a relationship without establishing that the relationship is meaningful, causal, desirable, or fair.
The data already contains history
One of the most important misconceptions about algorithmic fairness is the idea that bias appears only when someone explicitly programs a biased rule.
Modern machine-learning systems usually learn from existing data. That data was produced by people and institutions operating under particular social and economic conditions.

If historical hiring favored certain institutions, a hiring dataset can contain that pattern. If access to credit differed across communities, historical lending data can contain those differences. If educational opportunities were unequal, academic records can reflect those inequalities.
The algorithm may reproduce a pattern without anyone explicitly telling it to discriminate.

This is why removing a sensitive variable does not necessarily remove its influence. Other variables can contain related information. Location, education, employment history, school attended, language, and many other features can act as proxies for social circumstances.

The problem is not that every correlated variable must be removed. Many legitimate variables are correlated with other characteristics. The problem is that correlation can hide assumptions that the institution never intended to examine.
Accuracy is not fairness
Suppose an algorithm predicts loan default with very high accuracy.
That tells us something important about prediction. It does not tell us whether the resulting decisions are fair.
A system can be accurate overall while making different kinds of errors for different groups. It can also optimize an objective that is itself inappropriate.
This creates a fundamental distinction between technical performance and social acceptability.
Accuracy asks whether the prediction is usually correct. Fairness asks whether the decision process and its consequences are acceptable.
Those are related questions, but they are not interchangeable.
There is no single definition of fairness
Consider a system that evaluates applicants from two groups.

We might want both groups to have similar approval rates. We might instead want similar false-positive and false-negative rates. We might want a given risk score to have the same meaning across groups. We might want people with similar qualifications to receive similar treatment.
These goals are not always simultaneously achievable.
Fairness therefore cannot be reduced to one universal metric. Before engineers can optimize a fairness measure, institutions must decide what kind of equality matters for the decision.
That is partly a mathematical problem, but it is also a question of values and institutional purpose.
The objective matters
Every decision system optimizes something.

A lender may want to minimize default risk. A company may want to identify candidates likely to remain with the organization. A university may want to estimate academic outcomes. A fraud system may want to minimize financial losses.
These objectives are not automatically the same as the public purpose of the institution.

A bank maximizing repayment probability is not necessarily maximizing access to credit. A company minimizing turnover is not necessarily maximizing opportunity. A university predicting graduation is not necessarily measuring who deserves an education.
The algorithm can optimize the objective it is given. It cannot determine whether that objective is morally or institutionally appropriate.
The human in the loop is not enough
Organizations often describe automated systems as safe because a human remains involved.
But human involvement does not automatically mean meaningful oversight.

Suppose an algorithm ranks five hundred job applicants and highlights the top twenty. A recruiter is still technically making the final decision. But the recruiter is unlikely to examine all five hundred applications with equal attention.
The algorithm has therefore shaped the decision even without making it.
This is especially important because humans can develop automation bias: the tendency to place excessive confidence in automated recommendations.
Meaningful human oversight requires more than a person being present. The person must have enough authority, time, information, and expertise to question the system.
NIST identifies accountability, transparency, explainability, interpretability, reliability, privacy, and fairness with harmful bias managed as important characteristics of trustworthy AI. [1]
The black box problem
A black box is not simply a model that nobody understands.
A model can be mathematically specified while still being difficult to explain to the person affected by its output.
For an applicant, the important question is usually not how many parameters the model contains. It is: why did I receive this decision?
That requires a different kind of explanation. The person may need to know what information was considered, which factors mattered, whether an error occurred, and how the decision can be challenged.

Transparency therefore has several layers: transparency about the existence of the system, its purpose, its data, its evaluation, its limitations, its individual outputs, and the institution responsible for using it.
A credit decision has consequences
Consider an applicant denied credit by an automated or algorithm-assisted system.
Telling the applicant that an artificial intelligence system rejected the application is not a meaningful explanation.

In the United States, the CFPB has stated that creditors using complex algorithms must still comply with requirements to provide specific reasons for adverse credit decisions. The complexity of the model does not remove that obligation. [2][3]
This illustrates a broader principle: technical complexity cannot become an excuse for institutional opacity.
Accountability cannot disappear into the model
When an automated decision causes harm, responsibility can become fragmented.

The software company may blame the organization using the system. The organization may blame the vendor. The vendor may blame the training data. Engineers may say the model behaved according to its objective.
The person affected still has the same problem.
A system should never become a responsibility sink.

The organization that deploys a system must remain accountable for the consequences of using it. Developers have responsibilities concerning design, documentation, testing, limitations, and known failure modes. Operators need appropriate training and authority.
The exact distribution of responsibility can vary by system, but there must always be identifiable human and institutional accountability.
The right to challenge a decision
A consequential decision should not become an unbreakable wall simply because software produced it.
People need mechanisms to correct inaccurate information, provide additional evidence, request review, and challenge inappropriate decisions.
This is where explanation and accountability meet.
If a person cannot understand a decision, correcting an error becomes difficult. If nobody can identify who is responsible, an appeal becomes meaningless.
Contestability should therefore be treated as part of system design, not as an administrative feature added afterward.
When automation scales mistakes
Human decision-makers make mistakes. Algorithms do too.
The difference is scale.
A human may make a poor decision about one applicant. A deployed model can apply the same flawed logic to thousands or millions of people.
This is why automated systems require systematic testing and monitoring.
The question is not simply whether the model works on a test dataset. It is whether it continues to work in the environment where people actually depend on it.
The world changes after deployment
A model is trained on historical information, but the future is not required to resemble the past.
Economic conditions change. Hiring practices change. Educational systems change. Regulations change. User behavior changes.
A model that was reliable during development can become less reliable after deployment.
There is another complication: the system itself can change the data it later receives.

If an admissions model changes which students receive opportunities, the resulting student population changes. If a hiring system determines who gets hired, future employment data is partly shaped by the system.
The algorithm is no longer merely observing society. It is participating in it.
Prediction can become self-reinforcing
Suppose a system predicts that a student is unlikely to succeed in an advanced course.
The student is therefore not recommended for the course.
The student never receives the opportunity or resources associated with that course.
Later, the institution observes that the student did not succeed in that path.
The original prediction now appears justified.
But the prediction partly changed the conditions under which it was tested.
This is why predictive systems require special caution when their outputs influence future opportunities.
Fairness begins before training
A common mistake is to treat fairness as a model-level optimization problem.
The deeper questions come earlier.
Should this decision be automated at all?
What exactly are we predicting?
Why does that prediction matter?
Who can be harmed by an incorrect prediction?
Which errors are most serious?
Does the available data represent the people affected?
Can a person challenge the result?
These are system-design questions.
Regulation is moving toward risk
Regulatory approaches increasingly distinguish between low-consequence AI applications and systems that can significantly affect people's lives.

The European Union's AI Act places specific high-risk requirements on certain AI systems used in areas including employment, education, and creditworthiness. These requirements address areas such as risk management, data quality, documentation, human oversight, accuracy, robustness, and cybersecurity. [4]

Employment is another concrete example. New York City's rules for covered automated employment decision tools require a bias audit, publication of audit information, and notice to affected candidates or employees. [5]
The broader direction is significant: the more consequential the decision, the stronger the expectations around testing, transparency, oversight, and accountability.
But regulation cannot solve everything
Laws can define obligations, but they cannot automatically determine whether a particular model is socially desirable.
Nor can regulation replace engineering discipline.
A responsible system still needs careful data collection, validation, testing, monitoring, documentation, security, privacy protection, and failure analysis.
Governance and engineering therefore have to work together.
What a responsible algorithmic system requires
A responsible decision system should answer several questions before deployment.
First: what decision is the system supporting, and why is automation appropriate?
Second: what information does the system use, where did that information come from, and what limitations does it have?
Third: how does the system perform across the populations that will actually encounter it?
Fourth: what happens when the model is wrong?
Fifth: can affected people understand and challenge important decisions?
Sixth: who can stop the system, modify it, or override it?
Finally: who is accountable when the system causes harm?
These questions turn an algorithm from a mysterious component into an accountable part of an institution.
Trust should be earned
The right response to algorithmic systems is neither blind trust nor automatic rejection.

Some automated systems are useful precisely because they can process information at a scale humans cannot. They can identify patterns, reduce repetitive work, improve consistency, and support complex decisions.
But trust should depend on evidence.

A trustworthy system should have a clearly defined purpose, appropriate data, measurable performance, known limitations, meaningful monitoring, human oversight, and mechanisms for correction and appeal.
Most importantly, the institution using it must remain accountable.
The human should remain larger than the score
A student is not a probability of graduation.
A worker is not a retention score.
A borrower is not a default probability.
A job applicant is not a ranking position.
These representations can be useful. Institutions need abstractions to make decisions at scale. The danger begins when the abstraction becomes indistinguishable from the person.
The purpose of responsible algorithmic decision-making is therefore not to eliminate mathematical models from society.
It is to prevent those models from becoming invisible authorities.
The real question
The important question is not whether machines should make decisions.
Machines already participate in decisions across employment, finance, education, healthcare, security, commerce, and public administration.
The real question is how much authority we should give them, under what conditions, and with what safeguards.
An algorithm can calculate a probability.
It can rank a thousand candidates.
It can detect a pattern that no individual could see.
But the decision to give that calculation authority is still a human decision.
That is where accountability begins.
